notes.title: The definite articles o and a

blocks.text: A noun refers to a person, place or thing. Very few English nouns have a masculine or feminine form — host/hostess is a rare one — but every noun in Portuguese has a grammatical gender. The definite article, the, is o for masculine and a for feminine, and it reflects that gender.
People
Places and things have a gender too
But the ending doesn't always tell you
o and a are used far more often than the is in English, and they always tell you the gender. So when you learn a new noun, learn it with its article — not casa but a casa.
One and two are the numbers that change with gender: they agree with the noun they refer to. You'll meet the rest of the numbers in the next lesson.

blocks.text: Words ending in –a, –e, –o, or the consonants –s, –m or –ns are usually stressed on the second-to-last syllable.
Words ending in –i or –u (or –i/–u followed by –m or –s), or in a diphthong, are stressed on the last syllable.

If a word follows neither rule, a written accent marks the stressed syllable. On í and ú the acute simply marks stress; on á, é and ó it marks stress and an open vowel. The circumflex on â, ê and ô marks a closed vowel. The grave accent, used only on à in certain contractions, doesn't change stress at all.
A diphthong is two vowels making one sound together — the ei in seis (six) sounds like the a in hate.
They has a masculine and a feminine form: eles and elas. And Portuguese has no subject pronoun for it.
Ter is irregular. The accent on the second and third person plural doesn't change the pronunciation.

Filhos can mean four sons, or sons and daughters together. The same logic applies to friends: nós temos amigas is a group of women, while nós temos amigos is either all men or a mixed group.

blocks.text: In quarto the r is that breathy h, or a flap. Cariocas in Rio famously trill their r more; paulistanos in São Paulo soften it. In small towns it can be longer, close to the American r. These regional differences are rarely strong enough to confuse anyone — and newscasters everywhere speak a standard Brazilian Portuguese, much as they do in the U.S.

A means to. Contracted with the feminine article a it becomes à (to the / on the). You'll meet it properly in later lessons; for now just notice it.

rows: A escada rolante é à direita da porta.
The escalator is to the right of the door.
O banco é à esquerda do supermercado.
The bank is to the left of the supermarket.

blocks.text: No inversion and no auxiliary — unlike English, you just start the sentence with the question word.

rows: Quem é a pessoa à esquerda?
Who is the person on the left?

blocks.text: Ordinals are adjectives, so they agree in gender and number with the noun.

rows: O banco é no segundo quarteirão.
The bank is on the second block.

blocks.text: They're abbreviated with a superscript º for masculine and ª for feminine.

rows: O banheiro é a primeira porta à esquerda.

blocks.text: Que horas são? — What time is it?
Most regular infinitives end in –ar, –er or –ir, and each type follows its own pattern of endings. This lesson takes the –ar verbs, like falar (to speak).
Eu and nós can be dropped — the ending already says who the subject is. Estudo espanhol means I study Spanish; Estudamos matemática, We study math.
In sentences
More –ar verbs
Careful: aprender ends in –er, not –ar, so it doesn't take these endings. The book lists it here among the vocabulary, not as an –ar verb.

rows: Eu trabalho das oito da manhã às seis da tarde.
Ele toma banho antes das sete da manhã.
He takes a shower before 7:00 a.m.
Você encontra os seus amigos ao meio-dia.
You meet your friends at noon.
Tomamos café da manhã às sete e meia.

As provas terminam na semana que vem.
O piloto viaja três vezes por semana.
The pilot travels three times a week.

blocks.text: Que horas são? means What time is it? Unlike English, where the answer always starts with it is, in Portuguese ser agrees with hora.
Hora is feminine — uma hora, duas horas. Minuto is masculine — um minuto, dois minutos.

rows: É uma hora e dois minutos.

blocks.text: They can go before the main verb, or at the beginning or the end of a sentence.

blocks.text: Flávia writes home from college in Rio. Rather than reproduce the letter, here are the lines carrying the lesson — –ar verbs, clock times and frequency adverbs — plus the way a Brazilian signs off to family.

rows: Eu estou muito bem na faculdade aqui.

Frequentemente, eu acordo cedo e caminho na praia durante uma hora.
Often I wake up early and take a walk on the beach for an hour.
Depois eu tomo o café da manhã como você sempre aconselha.
After that I have breakfast, as you always advise.
As aulas são das nove da manhã às três da tarde.
Classes are from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.
Muitas vezes eu estudo na biblioteca das três às cinco.
I often study in the library from 3:00 to 5:00 p.m.
Duas vezes por semana, eu e a minha melhor amiga trabalhamos como voluntárias.
Twice a week, my best friend and I work as volunteers.
Às vezes, quando o tempo está bom, nós jogamos vôlei na praia.
Once in a while when the weather is good, we play beach volleyball.
No fim de semana há sempre uma festa.
On weekends there's always a party.
Eu mando abraços para eles e um beijo para você.
I send hugs to them and a kiss to you.
